![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14128562/assets/838fe13d4ad778c391ff628b508d17ed450b56e800180c946038be1ccfc5655e.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+2z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
question.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+2z⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14128562/assets/d47102fe8d01acf93fe0e6ef9017e06412e843ea64584b9f4e7151214aeb9197.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=3$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=3$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+6⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =x-y+6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x-y+6\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x-y+6\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}x-y+6\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-xy+6x]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{13}{2}-y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{13}{2}y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,x-y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =y-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}y-x\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}y-x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}y-x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[xy-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}y-\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}y]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =11+1 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$
